prompt: A service issues a large number of independent uniform random IDs. While collision risk is still small, it expects to issue twice as many IDs. What is the approximate effect on any-pair collision risk at the same ID width?

options.text: It grows roughly fourfold because the pair count grows roughly fourfold.
options.explanation: Small birthday risk is approximately the number of pairs divided by the space size.

options.text: It is unchanged until half the ID space is used.
options.explanation: Collisions matter well before the space is half filled.

options.text: It halves because more values are sampled.
options.explanation: More draws create more opportunities to collide.

options.text: It doubles exactly for every population size.
options.explanation: The all-pairs quantity grows approximately quadratically, and saturation eventually limits probability.

workedExample: Consider all existing pairs, not only the next draw against one target. The approximation concerns small probabilities and sufficiently large populations; for larger risk use the full collision model and plan duplicate handling.

prompt: Why is generic collision search against an ideal hash easier than matching one specified hash output?

options.text: A collision search needs no two distinct inputs.
options.explanation: The attack requires distinct inputs with the same output.

options.text: A hash’s output bit length guarantees no algorithm-specific weakness.
options.explanation: Cryptanalysis can beat the ideal generic bound.

options.text: The attacker must fill every possible output first.
options.explanation: A collision becomes likely around the square-root scale under the ideal model.

options.text: Any pair of outputs can satisfy the collision search.
options.explanation: Birthday search accumulates opportunities across all pairs rather than one fixed target.

workedExample: Identify the success event. Preimage search targets one prescribed output; collision search accepts any matching pair. That larger set of successful relationships explains the square-root generic work scale.
